entities.name: Dunkirk evacuation
entities.label: EventWindow
entities.summary:
The Dunkirk evacuation, also known as Operation Dynamo, was a pivotal naval operation that took place between May 26 and June 4, 1940, during the early stages of World War II. This massive rescue effort involved the evacuation of over 338,000 Allied soldiers from the beaches and harbour of Dunkirk, France, in the face of a relentless German advance. The operation was a testament to the bravery and ingenuity of the British military, who, despite being vastly outnumbered, managed to evacuate a significant portion of their forces, thereby preventing a catastrophic defeat. The Dunkirk evacuation was a significant turning point in the war, as it allowed the Allies to regroup and reorganize, ultimately contributing to their ultimate victory.

The evacuation was a complex and chaotic operation, involving a flotilla of over 800 boats and ships, including naval vessels, civilian boats, and even makeshift vessels constructed from anything available. The Germans, however, were closing in on the city, and the evacuation had to be carried out under intense pressure. Despite these challenges, the Allies managed to evacuate over 338,000 soldiers, although at a significant cost, with over 68,000 left behind and many more killed or wounded.

The Dunkirk evacuation had a profound impact on the course of the war, as it allowed the Allies to regroup and reorganize, ultimately contributing to their ultimate victory. The operation also marked a significant shift in the balance of power in Europe, as the British and French forces were able to hold off the German advance, at least temporarily. The evacuation also had a lasting impact on the British military, as it marked a turning point in their willingness to fight, and ultimately contributed to their determination to resist Nazi Germany.
